text: So at a glance, Braintrust as a platform is focused around agent quality.

text: And the core idea is helping teams build and maintain confidence with the AI features or the AI agents that they're shipping.

text: And there are two key pillars of agent quality.

text: The first is evals, which we talked about earlier.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Evals is what you do
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Before your agent reaches production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is when teams experiment, they test the behavior, and they build the confidence that they want to have before they ship to production.

text: Observability is once your agent is in production and is interfacing with real-life users, it's creating interactions, and the goal is to take that hypothesis that you built in your offline development process and then reinforce that in your production scenario through continuous monitoring.

text: You know, evals matter because LLMs by nature are non-deterministic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They are highly variable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That variability is exactly what makes them so powerful.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They can reason across many different domains.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They can solve different kinds of problems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they can handle a wide range of user needs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But that same flexibility also creates risk.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agents use LLM as their brain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And agentic experiences are starting to become the primary way in which users will interact with companies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So teams need confidence in their agents that they will behave reliably and produce the outcomes that they expect.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And without evals, companies face real risks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Brands become a risk if there's inconsistent behaviors, compliance if the agent says or does the wrong thing, and there's a cost and maintenance risk if the systems are hard or unreliable to debug or control.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The goal of evals is to reduce that uncertainty before launch so that customers have a good experience and the agents behave the way that you expect them to.

text: The important thing is that teams acknowledge that this is a real problem and they need a way to understand how agents behave based on different inputs.

text: At the simplest level, an eval system has three different criteria.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has a way to execute agents against test inputs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, a way to view the outputs or the scores, even if those are being logged in a spreadsheet.

text: And third, a set of test inputs or examples that can invoke the agent.

text: An input example is whatever information is needed to start the agent run.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It could be a prompt, a request, or context that causes the agent to act.

text: Now, spreadsheet-based evals are not wrong.

text: However, they're often the first step for a useful version of eval workflow.

text: And this is where things start to get complicated.

text: The underlying technology is complex.

text: LLMs are not simply deterministic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agent quality is a multi-persona problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's not just software engineers and AI engineers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There are PMs who used to build PRDs that are now running evals.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There are SMEs who have the domain expertise of the product that you're building.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And evals themselves are just one part of the development and operating workflow
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And gone are the days where you build once with unit tests and regression tests, you ship to production, and you don't think about it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Evals are a way for you to continue hill climbing against one target, which is agent quality.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's talk about the different stages of the eval platforms that we see.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And before we do that, this is the north star for many teams.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They want to build the improvement loop, which is I have a feature or application that's in production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I can observe the failure modes that happen based on dimensions that I define.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I want to be able to grab those failure modes and create test cases so that I can iterate offline, so I can improve my agent quality without introducing new regressions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then you continue iterating over time because just like in classical ML, drift becomes a real thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The way users interact with your agents will change over time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The way you build your agents will change over time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what does phase one look like?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There were some hands that were raised around spreadsheets and there's nothing to be shameful about.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is where many people start.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the basic setup is pretty simple.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a for loop with a set of input examples and a way to execute the agent.

text: And with that, you can run the same examples that you tweak and see how the agent responds with the outputs over time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The biggest advantage is accessibility and time.

text: You can start this with basically zero barrier to entry.

text: But the returns diminish pretty quickly.

text: At this stage, you're pretty much only documenting.

text: You can't really do true experimentation.

text: And let alone do any type of analysis over time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Common limitations are analytics are hard, they're manual, human scoring is valuable but difficult to do, collaboration is very weak, and domain experts are usually boxed out of these type of results.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So again, spreadsheets are a great starting place but difficult to evolve.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then someone, usually a product engineer, they see this problem and they think, OK, I can build a nice UI, a bespoke UI to help solve this problem.

text: But the limitation that you might have thought about, it continues.

text: And though iteration cycles become quicker, it is still not easy for users to persist that data and do long horizon analytics on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Still just a reporting tool.

text: I want to be able to tweak a system prompt.

text: And when we think, kind of going back to the flywheel, when we think about what are the best systems that enable this, well, you should be able to, starting at the top, observe the failure modes, log every input, output, every step of your trace execution that your agent takes, analyze, understand what went wrong.
